mcqs.question: Why does modeling spot assignment as a SpotAssignmentStrategy interface instead of an if/else inside ParkingLot matter?
options: It makes ParkingLot thread-safe automatically
It removes the need for a ParkingSpot class entirely
New assignment rules become new classes, so ParkingLot never has to change when a policy changes
It guarantees a spot is always found regardless of vehicle type
mcqs.explanation: The Strategy pattern's value here is isolating change: adding nearest-available vs size-matched vs EV-only assignment means writing a new class, not editing ParkingLot's logic. It doesn't affect thread-safety, doesn't remove ParkingSpot, and doesn't guarantee availability — a full lot is still a full lot.

mcqs.question: Two cars grab for 'the last compact spot' at the same instant. What actually fixes the race?
options: Make the spot-reservation step itself atomic (e.g. an atomic pop from the free-bucket), not just the search that finds a candidate spot
Add a five-second delay before assigning any spot
Only allow one car to enter the lot at a time, lot-wide
Have each car re-check availability after being assigned a spot
mcqs.explanation: The race exists because 'find' and 'mark' are two separate steps — both cars can find the same spot before either marks it. Collapsing them into one atomic operation (pop from the bucket) closes the race. A delay only narrows the window; serializing entry lot-wide kills throughput for something only one level's bucket needs; re-checking after assignment is too late.

mcqs.question: Why does a per-level, per-type free-spot index (a queue per SpotType) beat scanning level.getSpots() for an open spot?
options: It uses less memory than storing the spots at all
It removes the need for a Level class
It makes pricing calculations faster
Lookup cost stops depending on how many spots the level has — it becomes a queue pop, not a scan
mcqs.explanation: The index turns 'find a free spot of type X' from an O(spots) scan into an O(1) queue pop, which is the real performance win. It uses roughly the same memory (still tracking every spot), doesn't touch pricing, and Level is still needed as the owner of the index.

mcqs.question: For a large mall lot with four separate entrances, which spot-reservation approach scales better, and why?
options: Reserve an exact spot at entry, because drivers know exactly where to go
Reserve only a spot type at entry and assign the exact spot at walk-in, because it avoids cross-entrance coordination on a specific spot
Neither — multi-entrance lots should not support reservations at all
Reserve an exact spot at entry, because it's simpler to implement
mcqs.explanation: With four entrances potentially assigning spots concurrently, locking a specific spot at entry requires coordinating across all of them. Reserving only a type lets each entrance work against the shared type-bucket (already safe under atomic pop), deciding the exact spot later. Implementation simplicity doesn't outweigh the correctness risk at this scale.

mcqs.question: A driver parks for 61 minutes. Why is fee = hourlyRate * (exitTime - entryTime) with no stated rounding rule a design problem, not just a math nitpick?
options: It's not a problem — most billing systems round automatically with no configuration
It only matters for parking lots that charge a flat rate

Without a stated rounding/grace-period rule, the exact same 61-minute stay bills differently depending on incidental implementation details, which is invisible to the driver and a common source of disputes
It's fine because exitTime - entryTime is always exact to the millisecond
mcqs.explanation: The issue isn't the subtraction — it's the missing policy. Whether 61 minutes bills as 2 hours, 1.02 hours, or something else needs to be an explicit, stated rule (e.g. round up past a grace period), not an accident of the arithmetic. Billing systems don't round without a rule to round by, this isn't specific to flat-rate pricing, and millisecond precision doesn't resolve what to actually bill for it.
